For most of the twentieth century, domestic hot water was a small item in the heat budget of a Danish house. A typical older house with energy label D needs around 150 kWh of space heating per m² of floor area per year. Hot water adds 13 kWh/m², less than a tenth of the total.
Better houses have changed the picture (

). Insulation, airtightness and heat recovery ventilation have cut the space heating demand of a passive house to 15 kWh/m², and of a house in the Danish low-energy class to about 10 kWh/m². The hot water demand has not changed, because it depends on the people living in the house and not on its envelope. A family takes the same showers in a passive house as in a house from 1965. In a passive house hot water is therefore close to half of the heat demand, and in a low-energy class house it is more than half.

children.alt: Horizontal stacked bar chart of net heat demand per m² floor area per year. A house with energy label D has 150 kWh/m² of space heating and 13 kWh/m² of hot water, so hot water is 8 %. A passive house has 15 kWh/m² of space heating, so hot water is 46 %. A house in the Danish low-energy class has 10 kWh/m² of space heating, so hot water is 57 %.

The Danish energy frame calculation (Be18) uses a fixed hot water demand of 250 L per m² of heated floor area per year, heated from 10 °C to 55 °C
. With the average properties of water between 10 °C and 55 °C this is

However, measured hot water use varies by a factor of two or three between households of the same size, and it depends much more on the number of occupants, their age and their habits than on the floor area.

The temperature also matters. A floor heating system in a low-energy house runs at 30–35 °C (Chapter C1). Hot water must be stored at 50–55 °C or more to keep Legionella bacteria from growing. When the same heat pump supplies both, the hot water is the expensive part of its work, because the efficiency of a heat pump falls as the temperature it delivers rises. In an all-electric low-energy house, hot water can easily use as much electricity as space heating.

There are two ways to cut the cost of hot water, and this chapter is built around them:

- **Use less heat.** Shower water leaves the house at about 30 °C, at the same moment as cold water comes in. A drain water heat recovery unit passes that heat to the incoming cold water. This is Part A of the chapter.
- **Buy the heat at the right time.** Electricity prices vary over the day, with a peak in the early evening, which is exactly when many families shower. A well-sized hot water tank can be charged in cheap hours and emptied in expensive ones. This is Part B.

The next section sets out how much hot water a dwelling uses and how fast it is drawn, which both parts build on.

These powers are far larger than anything else in the heating system of a low-energy house. The whole house may need only 2–3 kW of space heating on the coldest day, and a heat pump sized for that cannot heat a shower as it runs. There are two ways out:
District heating can deliver 30–40 kW through a heat exchanger in a flat station, so the water is heated as it is used and nothing is stored.

A heat pump or a small boiler heats a tank slowly, over hours, and the tank delivers the high power during the tapping. The tank decouples the power the heat source must deliver from the power the user draws.

Storage is what makes it possible to choose *when* the heat source runs, which is the topic of Part B. Showers are what make drain water heat recovery worthwhile, which is the topic of Part A. They are the largest single hot water use in most homes, and they are the one use where the warm waste water flows to the drain at the same moment as the cold water comes in.
The cold water temperature is on average 10 C, which is ok for most calculations, but actually fluctuates between 8-17 C throughout the year.
1 L of water warmed by 1 K takes about 1.15 Wh. 100 L warmed by 45 K takes about 5 kWh.
One 8-minute shower uses about 60 L of 40 °C water, which is 40 L of 55 °C water and about 2 kWh of heat.
Hot water use is about 30–40 L of 55 °C water per person per day, or about 550–750 kWh per person per year before losses.
The Be18 calculation value is 13 kWh/m² per year, about 2000 kWh per year for a 150 m² house.
A shower draws about 15–20 kW while it runs, several times the design heat load of a low-energy house.
Four types of hot water heater are common in Danish single-family houses. They differ in where the heat comes from and in what else the unit does.

A tank with an electric heating element and a thermostat. Each kWh of hot water costs one kWh of electricity, plus the standing loss of the tank, which is set by the insulation and the tank temperature. The electric water heater is the reference for the other solutions in this book.
The range runs from 14 to 288 L, insulated with polyurethane foam, with a thermostat that can be set up to about 65 °C

A tank with a small air-to-water heat pump on top. The heat pump takes its air through ducts, either outdoor air or exhaust air from the house. The COP at an air temperature of 20 °C is typically around 3 to 4. With outdoor air, the COP falls in winter, when the air is cold. With exhaust air, the heat source is close to room temperature all year, but the air flow is limited by the ventilation.
The MetroAir Aqua heats a tank of 190 or 260 L with 1.6 kW of heat pump capacity. The COP is 3.7 and 4.1 at an air temperature of 20 °C for the two tank sizes
Heat pump for space heating and hot water.

An air-to-water or ground source heat pump that serves both the floor heating and a hot water tank, often built into the indoor unit. The heat pump switches between floor heating at about 35 °C and charging the tank at 50–55 °C. The COP is lower when it heats hot water than when it heats the floor, because the condensing temperature is higher. The share of the year’s heat that goes to hot water grows as the space heating demand falls, so in a low-energy house the COP for hot water matters as much as the SCOP for space heating.

An air-to-water heat pump with an outdoor unit of 2 to 18 kW and the natural refrigerant R290. The SCOP is up to 6.22 at a flow temperature of 35 °C (EN 14825, average climate), and the flow temperature can reach 75 °C
. With the HYDRO C2 indoor unit, the hot water tank is built into the indoor unit.

A compact unit combines balanced ventilation with heat recovery, an exhaust-air heat pump and a hot water tank in one cabinet. The heat pump takes heat from the exhaust air after the heat exchanger and uses it for the hot water and, in some units, the supply air. The heat source is limited by the ventilation air flow, so the unit suits houses with a small heating demand, such as passive houses. Because ventilation, heat pump and tank share one cabinet, the parts are harder to reach and replace than in separate units, and a fault in one part can take ventilation and hot water out of service together.
The Compact P has a 180 L tank in a cabinet of 900 × 610 × 2065 mm. The counterflow heat exchanger has a temperature efficiency of up to 95 %
. The unit is certified as a Passive House component at air flows of
The Danish Energy Agency keeps an official list of heat pumps sold in Denmark, Varmepumpelisten, with the tested efficiency of each product
. It is the place to compare heat pumps of the types above.

The saving from charging at night depends on the heat source. With an electric water heater, the family uses 5.7 kWh of electricity a day for hot water, and charging at 00–06 instead of at the time of use reduces the cost by 6.6 DKK on this day. With a heat pump at a COP of 2.5, the reduction is 2.6 DKK a day. Both values are upper limits, since they are based on a single day with a large price spread, neglect the standing loss, and assume a heat source that can deliver the shower power directly. Over a year, the saving is of the order of a few thousand DKK with a resistance heater and about a thousand DKK with a heat pump.

Sizing the tank as a thermal battery

children.label: Sizing the tank as a thermal battery

children.value: A hot water tank is a battery for heat. When it is charged, the heat source runs. When hot water is drawn, the tank delivers. If the tank is big enough, the two no longer have to happen at the same time, and the heat pump can run in the hours when electricity is cheap or has a low primary energy factor. The question is how big “big enough” is.

The method is a first estimate. It assumes the tank is either hot or cold, with a fixed usable fraction, and that the heat source charges evenly over its allowed hours. In a real tank, the thermocline grows while the tank sits, the heat pump is switched by a thermostat at a sensor partway up the tank, and the standing loss depends on how much of the tank is hot. The tank simulator in
handles all of this, so the hand estimate should always be checked there.

With the default 3 kW heat pump and a sensor at 60 % of the tank height, the simulator gives:
0.36 kWh: the evening shower runs cold
0.02 kWh: the kitchen tap at 22:00 is slightly below 45 °C
0.18 kWh: the second morning shower runs cold
0.01 kWh: the kitchen tap at 07:15 is slightly below 45 °C

In both cases the hand estimate is close: the tank it gives delivers every shower at full temperature and falls just short only for one small kitchen tapping right after a peak. One standard size up, it is safe. A smaller tank fails where the method says it will, at the peak that sets the size. Note that the night-charged tank loses less than half of the standing loss we assumed, because it is cold for much of the evening. The uniform case works for a different reason than the method assumes: the heat pump does not charge evenly at 0.28 kW. A thermostat starts it at full power when the sensor has cooled, and during the morning showers its 3 kW output helps cover the draw.
1 kWh stored at 55 °C, counted from 10 °C cold water, needs about 20 L of water, or 23 L with a usable fraction of 0.85.
Charging only at night means storing a full day of hot water: about 40–45 L per person.
Charging whenever needed, with a thermostat, needs about 20–25 L per person, enough to cover the largest peak.
The heat pump must deliver at least the daily heat divided by the number of allowed hours, plus a margin.

In an apartment building, hot water is produced centrally, in a district heating substation with a tank or a plate heat exchanger, and distributed to the flats through risers. Without circulation, the water in a riser cools between tappings, and the user has to run the tap until hot water arrives. A circulation loop prevents this. A pump keeps the hot water moving through the supply pipes and back to the substation, so that the whole network stays hot at all hours. The return of the loop is kept above 50 °C to limit the growth of Legionella.

Measurements show that the loss is large. In Danish apartment buildings, circulation losses were 23–70 % of the heat delivered to the hot water system, and 54–89 % in office buildings

. In 134 Swedish multi-family buildings, the measured loss ranged from 0.5 to 76 kWh per m² of heated floor area per year. The mean was 14 kWh/m² in older buildings and 6 kWh/m² in newer ones, against an assumed 4 kWh/m²
